claim: 61 ancient South American camelid mitochondrial genomes were generated from samples dated between 3,500 and 2,400 years before the present from the Early Formative period.
source: In this study, we generated mitochondrial genomes for 61 ancient South American camelids dated between 3,500 and 2,400 years before the present (Early Formative period) from two archaeological sites in Northern Chile (Tulán-54 and Tulán-85), as well as 66 modern camelid mitogenomes and 815 modern mitochondrial control region sequences from across South America.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of ancient mitogenomes generated and their temporal range, supported by the study's own data collection and sequencing efforts.

claim: 66 modern camelid mitogenomes were generated from samples collected across South America.
source: In this study, we generated mitochondrial genomes for 61 ancient South American camelids dated between 3,500 and 2,400 years before the present (Early Formative period) from two archaeological sites in Northern Chile (Tulán-54 and Tulán-85), as well as 66 modern camelid mitogenomes and 815 modern mitochondrial control region sequences from across South America.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of modern mitogenomes generated as part of the study's data collection.

claim: 815 modern mitochondrial control region sequences were generated from South American camelids.
source: In this study, we generated mitochondrial genomes for 61 ancient South American camelids dated between 3,500 and 2,400 years before the present (Early Formative period) from two archaeological sites in Northern Chile (Tulán-54 and Tulán-85), as well as 66 modern camelid mitogenomes and 815 modern mitochondrial control region sequences from across South America.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of modern control region sequences generated as part of the study's data collection.

claim: A substantial proportion of ancient vicuña genetic variation has been lost since the Early Formative period.
source: A comparative analysis of these data suggests that a substantial proportion of the ancient vicuña genetic variation has been lost since the Early Formative period, as it is not present in modern specimens.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analysis of ancient and modern genetic data showing differences in genetic variation between time periods.

claim: An ancient guanaco population that no longer exists contributed to the domestication of South American camelids.
source: Moreover, we propose a domestication hypothesis that includes an ancient guanaco population that no longer exists.
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenetic analysis of ancient and modern mitogenomes showing extinct lineages.

claim: Interbreeding practices were widespread during the domestication process by early camelid herders in the Atacama during the Early Formative period.
source: Finally, we find evidence that interbreeding practices were widespread during the domestication process by the early camelid herders in the Atacama during the Early Formative period and predating the Spanish conquest.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic evidence showing hybridization patterns in ancient samples from the Early Formative period.

claim: Interbreeding practices predated the Spanish conquest.
source: Finally, we find evidence that interbreeding practices were widespread during the domestication process by the early camelid herders in the Atacama during the Early Formative period and predating the Spanish conquest.
evidence: The claim is supported by the temporal dating of ancient samples showing hybridization before the Spanish conquest period.

claim: There are currently four camelid species inhabiting South America.
source: There are currently four camelid species inhabiting South America: two wild species, guanaco (Lama guanicoe) and vicuña (Vicugna vicugna), and two domestic species, llama (Lama glama) and alpaca (Vicugna pacos).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the current taxonomy of South American camelids.

claim: Guanaco (Lama guanicoe) and vicuña (Vicugna vicugna) are wild camelid species.
source: There are currently four camelid species inhabiting South America: two wild species, guanaco (Lama guanicoe) and vicuña (Vicugna vicugna), and two domestic species, llama (Lama glama) and alpaca (Vicugna pacos).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the classification of South American camelids.

claim: Llama (Lama glama) and alpaca (Vicugna pacos) are domestic camelid species.
source: There are currently four camelid species inhabiting South America: two wild species, guanaco (Lama guanicoe) and vicuña (Vicugna vicugna), and two domestic species, llama (Lama glama) and alpaca (Vicugna pacos).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the classification of South American camelids.

claim: Guanaco and vicuña are the most important endemic large herbivores in South America due to their ecological dominance in the upper Andean ecosystem.
source: Guanaco and vicuña are the most important endemic large herbivores in South America due to their ecological dominance in the upper Andean ecosystem and their importance for human populations in terms of their subsistence strategies (Muñoz and Mondini, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Muñoz and Mondini, 2008.

claim: Guanaco and vicuña are important for human populations in terms of their subsistence strategies.
source: Guanaco and vicuña are the most important endemic large herbivores in South America due to their ecological dominance in the upper Andean ecosystem and their importance for human populations in terms of their subsistence strategies (Muñoz and Mondini, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Muñoz and Mondini, 2008.

claim: Llama and alpaca first appeared in the fossil record around 7,000 years before the present.
source: Llama and alpaca first appeared in the fossil record around 7,000 years before the present (yr BP) as the result of domestication carried out by human communities across the Andes (Pires-Ferreira et al., 1976; Wheeler, 1984; Wheeler, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pires-Ferreira et al., 1976; Wheeler, 1984; Wheeler, 1995.

claim: Llama and alpaca appeared in the fossil record as the result of domestication carried out by human communities across the Andes.
source: Llama and alpaca first appeared in the fossil record around 7,000 years before the present (yr BP) as the result of domestication carried out by human communities across the Andes (Pires-Ferreira et al., 1976; Wheeler, 1984; Wheeler, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pires-Ferreira et al., 1976; Wheeler, 1984; Wheeler, 1995.

claim: Identifying domestic camelid species (alpaca and llama) in archaeological sites based solely on morphological data is challenging due to their similarity with wild ancestors.
source: Identifying the domestic species (alpaca and llama) in archaeological sites based solely on morphological data is challenging due to their similarity with respect to their wild ancestors.
evidence: This is a well-established challenge in zooarchaeology based on the morphological similarity between domestic and wild camelids.

claim: Using genetic methods to identify domestic camelid species presents challenges due to the hybridization history of the domestic species.
source: Using genetic methods also presents challenges due to the hybridization history of the domestic species, which are thought to have extensively hybridized following the Spanish conquest of South America that resulted in camelids slaughtered en masse.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about post-conquest hybridization in South American camelids.

claim: Domestic camelid species are thought to have extensively hybridized following the Spanish conquest of South America.
source: Using genetic methods also presents challenges due to the hybridization history of the domestic species, which are thought to have extensively hybridized following the Spanish conquest of South America that resulted in camelids slaughtered en masse.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about post-conquest hybridization in South American camelids.

claim: Camelids were slaughtered en masse following the Spanish conquest of South America.
source: Using genetic methods also presents challenges due to the hybridization history of the domestic species, which are thought to have extensively hybridized following the Spanish conquest of South America that resulted in camelids slaughtered en masse.
evidence: The claim is based on historical knowledge about the impact of Spanish conquest on camelid populations.

claim: Ancient samples were collected from Tulán-54 and Tulán-85 archaeological sites in Northern Chile.
source: In this study, we generated mitochondrial genomes for 61 ancient South American camelids dated between 3,500 and 2,400 years before the present (Early Formative period) from two archaeological sites in Northern Chile (Tulán-54 and Tulán-85), as well as 66 modern camelid mitogenomes and 815 modern mitochondrial control region sequences from across South America.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the sampling locations for ancient DNA.

claim: 47 ancient samples were collected from Tulán-54.
source: Using a capture strategy to enrich our aDNA libraries for mitochondrial sequences, we generated 61 near complete mitogenome sequences from camelid bone samples collected in the Tulán ravine and Atacama Salar: 47 from Tulán-54, 12 from Tulán-85, 1 from Tulán-94, and 1 from Tulán-52.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of samples from each archaeological site.

claim: 12 ancient samples were collected from Tulán-85.
source: Using a capture strategy to enrich our aDNA libraries for mitochondrial sequences, we generated 61 near complete mitogenome sequences from camelid bone samples collected in the Tulán ravine and Atacama Salar: 47 from Tulán-54, 12 from Tulán-85, 1 from Tulán-94, and 1 from Tulán-52.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of samples from each archaeological site.

claim: 1 ancient sample was collected from Tulán-94.
source: Using a capture strategy to enrich our aDNA libraries for mitochondrial sequences, we generated 61 near complete mitogenome sequences from camelid bone samples collected in the Tulán ravine and Atacama Salar: 47 from Tulán-54, 12 from Tulán-85, 1 from Tulán-94, and 1 from Tulán-52.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of samples from each archaeological site.

claim: 1 ancient sample was collected from Tulán-52.
source: Using a capture strategy to enrich our aDNA libraries for mitochondrial sequences, we generated 61 near complete mitogenome sequences from camelid bone samples collected in the Tulán ravine and Atacama Salar: 47 from Tulán-54, 12 from Tulán-85, 1 from Tulán-94, and 1 from Tulán-52.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of samples from each archaeological site.

claim: The average depth of coverage in the assembled ancient mitogenomes ranged between 2.53x and 153.03x.
source: The average depth of coverage in the assembled mitogenomes ranged between 2.53x and 153.03x with a final length of 15,438 base pair (bp).
evidence: The manuscript reports sequencing depth statistics from the ancient DNA sequencing data.

claim: The final length of assembled ancient mitogenomes was 15,438 base pairs.
source: The average depth of coverage in the assembled mitogenomes ranged between 2.53x and 153.03x with a final length of 15,438 base pair (bp).
evidence: The manuscript reports the length of the assembled mitogenomes from sequencing data.

claim: All ancient DNA samples showed the characteristic pattern of ancient DNA consistent with postmortem deamination damage.
source: The analysis with mapDamage showed the characteristic pattern of ancient DNA consistent with postmortem deamination damage in all aDNA samples (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports mapDamage analysis results showing DNA damage patterns typical of ancient DNA, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: An increasing presence of C-T and G-A mutations at the terminal ends of sequenced molecules was detected at the 5´-ends and 3´termini, respectively.
source: An increasing presence of C-T and G-A mutations at the terminal ends of sequenced molecules was detected at the 5´-ends and 3´termini, respectively, as expected from the damage model used, generating an excess of cytosine deaminations at single-strands ends of the DNA templates.
evidence: The manuscript reports specific DNA damage patterns observed in the ancient samples.

claim: The Bayesian phylogenetic analysis resulted in strong statistical support for four clades.
source: The Bayesian phylogenetic analysis of the ancient and modern mitogenomes using the Bactrian camel as outgroup resulted in strong statistical support for four clades in our data (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of phylogenetic analysis with reference to Figure 3.

claim: Clades 1, 2, and 3 form a large monophyletic clade supported by a posterior probability of one.
source: Clades 1, 2, and 3 form a large monophyletic clade supported by a posterior probability of one with all modern domestic camelids located in Clades 1 and 3.
evidence: The manuscript reports phylogenetic relationships with statistical support values.

claim: All modern domestic camelids are located in Clades 1 and 3.
source: Clades 1, 2, and 3 form a large monophyletic clade supported by a posterior probability of one with all modern domestic camelids located in Clades 1 and 3.
evidence: The manuscript reports the phylogenetic placement of modern domestic camelids.

claim: Clade 1 consists of a mixture of modern llama and alpaca mitogenomes and 20 ancient samples.
source: Clade 1 consists of a mixture of modern llama and alpaca mitogenomes and 20 ancient samples (3 from Tulán-85, 16 from Tulán-54, and 1 from Tulán-52) with 13 individuals morphologically identified as large sized animals and 1 specimen as small sized.
evidence: The manuscript describes the composition of Clade 1 based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Most modern guanacos grouped within Clade 2.
source: Most modern guanacos grouped within Clade 2, together with five samples from Tulán-54 morphologically identified as big sized and three samples as small sized animals.
evidence: The manuscript describes the composition of Clade 2 based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Clade 3 consists of both domestic camelid species and includes one modern guanaco.
source: Clade 3 consists of both domestic camelid species and includes one modern guanaco, as well as five ancient samples (C44, C5, C77, C52, and C48) that are closer to the ancestral mitogenome of the big clade.
evidence: The manuscript describes the composition of Clade 3 based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Clade 4 was supported by a posterior probability of one and grouped the majority of modern wild V. vicugna and two alpacas.
source: Clade 4 was supported by a posterior probability of one and grouped the majority of modern wild V. vicugna and two alpacas (V. pacos) (A_1557_alpaca and A03_alpaca).
evidence: The manuscript describes the composition of Clade 4 based on phylogenetic analysis with statistical support.

claim: The haplotype diversity for the ancient samples was 1.00.
source: The haplotype diversity for the ancient samples was 1.00 and for the modern samples, the values oscillated within 0.971–0.993 (Table S8).
evidence: The manuscript reports haplotype diversity statistics calculated from the genetic data.

claim: The haplotype diversity for modern samples oscillated within 0.971–0.993.
source: The haplotype diversity for the ancient samples was 1.00 and for the modern samples, the values oscillated within 0.971–0.993 (Table S8).
evidence: The manuscript reports haplotype diversity statistics calculated from the genetic data.

claim: Clade 4 (vicugnas) diverged first from the rest of the SACs at ~1.01–1.18 Myr.
source: Clade 4 (vicugnas) diverged first from the rest of the SACs at ~1.01–1.18 Myr.
evidence: The manuscript reports divergence time estimates from the dated BEAST phylogeny.

claim: Clade 3 forms at ~159–201 kyr following the first divergence.
source: Following the first divergence, Clade 3 forms at ~159–201 kyr with the final split forming Clades 1 and 2 at ~164–198 kyr.
evidence: The manuscript reports divergence time estimates from the dated BEAST phylogeny.

claim: The final split forming Clades 1 and 2 occurred at ~164–198 kyr.
source: Following the first divergence, Clade 3 forms at ~159–201 kyr with the final split forming Clades 1 and 2 at ~164–198 kyr.
evidence: The manuscript reports divergence time estimates from the dated BEAST phylogeny.

claim: The Bayesian Skyline Plot shows an increase in the Ne of the domesticated clades (Clades 1 and 3) around 8,000–6,000 yr BP in accordance with the putative initiation of domestication.
source: The Bayesian Skyline Plot (BSP) obtained from modern and ancient maternal sequences shows an increase in the Ne of the domesticated clades (Clades 1 and 3) around 8,000–6,000 yr BP in accordance with the putative initiation of domestication.
evidence: The manuscript reports demographic analysis results from the Bayesian Skyline Plot with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Clade 2 (guanacos) and Clade 4 (vicuñas) present evidence of a demographic expansion around 50,000 yr BP.
source: Clade 2 (guanacos) and Clade 4 (vicuñas) also present evidence of a demographic expansion, however at a much earlier time ~ 50,000 yr BP (Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports demographic analysis results from the Bayesian Skyline Plot with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Clades 2 and 4 show a modern demographic expansion around the domestication time, albeit less pronounced than for Clades 1 and 3.
source: Nevertheless, these two clades also show a modern demographic expansion, albeit less pronounced than for Clades 1 and 3, around the domestication time.
evidence: The manuscript reports demographic analysis results comparing different clades.

claim: Among the 849 samples analyzed for the control region, 76 different polymorphic sites and 158 haplotypes were detected.
source: Among the 849 samples analyzed, we detected 76 different polymorphic sites and 158 haplotypes divided into two main haplogroups (Figure 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports genetic diversity statistics from control region analysis with reference to Figure 5.

claim: The 158 haplotypes are divided into two main haplogroups.
source: Among the 849 samples analyzed, we detected 76 different polymorphic sites and 158 haplotypes divided into two main haplogroups (Figure 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports the structure of haplotype diversity with reference to Figure 5.

claim: Thirteen haplotypes were exclusively found in ancient samples.
source: Thirteen haplotypes were exclusively found in ancient samples, and eleven clustering with the Lama guanicoe and domestic camelid haplogroups: cacsilensis (66), cacsilensis-guanicoe (30), guanicoe (76), llamas (25), and alpacas (5) (Table S7).
evidence: The manuscript reports haplotype distribution patterns between ancient and modern samples.

claim: Only 11 haplotypes were shared by ancient and modern SAC despite the inclusion of a much higher number of modern mitochondrial sequences than ancient ones.
source: In total, 849 sequences were included, yielding 158 different haplotypes (42 from ancient sequences and 150 from modern sequences) of which only 11 haplotypes were shared by ancient and modern SAC despite the inclusion of a much higher number of modern mitochondrial sequences than ancient ones (Figure 6).
evidence: The manuscript reports haplotype sharing patterns between ancient and modern samples with reference to Figure 6.

claim: Most of the shared haplotypes belong to L. guanicoe guanicoe and Lama glama haplogroups.
source: Most of the shared haplotypes belong to L. guanicoe guanicoe and Lama glama haplogroups.
evidence: The manuscript reports the taxonomic distribution of shared haplotypes.

claim: The temporal network suggests a loss of ancient mitochondrial lineages, mostly in the vicuña.
source: The temporal network suggests a loss of ancient mitochondrial lineages, mostly in the vicuña (Table S9).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of temporal network analysis showing lineage loss.

claim: Control region haplotype diversity values were relatively similar between the modern samples (0.9765) and the ancient samples (0.9348).
source: Control region haplotype diversity values were relatively similar between the modern samples (0.9765) and the ancient samples (0.9348).
evidence: The manuscript reports haplotype diversity statistics for control region data.

claim: The ancient samples present a high genetic variation given their sample size as their diversity measures fall in the 93rd and 94th percentile of the distribution of the random samples from modern animals.
source: The analysis of all the data (i.e. without differentiating between large and small animals) indicated that the ancient samples do indeed present a high genetic variation given their sample size as their diversity measures fall in the 93rd and 94th percentile of the distribution of the random samples from modern animals (Figure 7A and D).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results comparing ancient and modern genetic diversity with reference to Figure 7.

claim: For the large animals, the ancient samples fall in the 89th and 95th percentile of the distribution of random samples from the modern Lama.
source: For the large animals, we observed that the ancient samples fall in the 89th and 95th percentile of the distribution of random samples from the modern Lama, while for the small animals, the ancient samples fall in the 98th percentile of the distribution of random samples of Vicugna for both statistics.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results comparing ancient and modern genetic diversity for different size classes.

claim: For the small animals, the ancient samples fall in the 98th percentile of the distribution of random samples of Vicugna for both statistics.
source: For the large animals, we observed that the ancient samples fall in the 89th and 95th percentile of the distribution of random samples from the modern Lama, while for the small animals, the ancient samples fall in the 98th percentile of the distribution of random samples of Vicugna for both statistics.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results comparing ancient and modern genetic diversity for different size classes.

claim: Morphometric analysis of the astragalus and anterior and posterior phalanx shows two differentiated groups based on body size, small sized and big sized individuals.
source: Morphometric analysis of the astragalus and anterior and posterior phalanx shows two differentiated groups based on body size, small sized and big sized individuals, consistent with observations in the wild Lama guanicoe and Vicugna vicugna (Wing, 1972; Kent, 1986; Elkin et al., 1991; Cartajena, 2003; Cartajena et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript reports morphometric analysis results with citations to previous studies.

claim: The small sized cluster most likely represents alpaca and vicuña specimens.
source: The small sized cluster most likely represents alpaca and vicuña specimens, while guanaco and llama individuals most likely form the big sized cluster.
evidence: The manuscript infers taxonomic identity from morphometric clustering patterns.

claim: Guanaco and llama individuals most likely form the big sized cluster.
source: The small sized cluster most likely represents alpaca and vicuña specimens, while guanaco and llama individuals most likely form the big sized cluster.
evidence: The manuscript infers taxonomic identity from morphometric clustering patterns.

claim: Archaeological measurements are consistent with modern camelids measurements.
source: Archaeological measurements are consistent with modern camelids measurements (shown in Figure 2; Cartajena, 2003; L' Heureux, 2010).
evidence: The manuscript reports comparison of archaeological and modern morphometric data with reference to Figure 2 and citations.

claim: A statistical comparison of the two groups (large vs. small sized animals) for either of the bones measured showed significant differences between the two groups of camelids (all p-values smaller than 10E-4).
source: A statistical comparison of the two groups (i.e. large vs. small sized animals) for either of the bones measured (i.e. first anterior phalanx, astragalus) showed significant differences between the two groups of camelids (all p-values smaller than 10E-4).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical test results comparing morphometric measurements between size groups.

claim: The astragalus and phalanx have a good discriminatory power to differentiate between larger (Lama) animals and the small (Vicugna) animals.
source: The bone morphological analyses implemented here indicate that the astragalus and phalanx have a good discriminatory power to differentiate between larger (Lama) animals and the small (Vicugna) animals (Figure 2a and b).
evidence: The manuscript reports the effectiveness of morphometric analysis for taxonomic discrimination with reference to Figure 2.

claim: The phylogeny places the vast majority of the ancient samples on the expected clades based on bone morphology.
source: The phylogeny generated using 130 ancient and modern camelid mitogenomes places the vast majority of the ancient samples on the expected clades based on bone morphology (Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports concordance between morphological and genetic taxonomic assignments with reference to Figure 3.

claim: 95% of large sized animal bone samples were grouped with modern samples of Lama.
source: Namely, the large sized animal bone samples were grouped with modern samples of Lama (95%) with the exception of two samples that grouped with the Vicugna vicugna clade (Clade 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of concordance between morphological and genetic taxonomic assignments.

claim: Two large sized animal bone samples grouped with the Vicugna vicugna clade (Clade 4).
source: Namely, the large sized animal bone samples were grouped with modern samples of Lama (95%) with the exception of two samples that grouped with the Vicugna vicugna clade (Clade 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports discordance between morphological and genetic taxonomic assignments for specific samples.

claim: 63% of small sized animal bone samples clustered in Clade 4.
source: The converse also occurred with the majority of the small sized animal bone samples that clustered in Clade 4 (63%) with the exception of seven (C77, C69 C70,C1, C12 from Tulán-54 and C65, C6 from Tulán-85) that grouped with Lama (Clades 2 and 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of concordance between morphological and genetic taxonomic assignments for small animals.

claim: Seven small sized animal bone samples grouped with Lama (Clades 2 and 3).
source: The converse also occurred with the majority of the small sized animal bone samples that clustered in Clade 4 (63%) with the exception of seven (C77, C69 C70,C1, C12 from Tulán-54 and C65, C6 from Tulán-85) that grouped with Lama (Clades 2 and 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports discordance between morphological and genetic taxonomic assignments for specific samples.

claim: Modern alpaca, with the exception of two samples, are located within the genus Lama alongside guanaco, modern llamas, and zooarchaeological samples of both large- and small sized animals.
source: Our analyses place modern alpaca, with the exception of two samples, within the genus Lama alongside guanaco, modern llamas, and zooarchaeological samples of both large- and small sized animals.
evidence: The manuscript reports phylogenetic placement of alpacas based on mitogenomic analysis.

claim: Llamas are a paraphyletic group with two main branches (Clades 1 and 3) within the greater Lama clade.
source: While llamas are a paraphyletic group with two main branches (Clades 1 and 3) within the greater Lama clade.
evidence: The manuscript reports phylogenetic relationships of llamas based on mitogenomic analysis.

claim: Within Clades 1 and 3, alpaca groups within llamas supporting the hypothesis that llamas and alpacas were both domesticated from guanacos.
source: Within Clades 1 and 3, alpaca groups within llamas supporting the hypothesis that llamas and alpacas were both domesticated from guanacos (hypothesis 3) while vicuña was possibly never domesticated.
evidence: The manuscript infers domestication history from phylogenetic relationships.

claim: Vicuña was possibly never domesticated.
source: Within Clades 1 and 3, alpaca groups within llamas supporting the hypothesis that llamas and alpacas were both domesticated from guanacos (hypothesis 3) while vicuña was possibly never domesticated.
evidence: The manuscript infers domestication history from phylogenetic relationships.

claim: The wild component of Clade 3 is now extinct.
source: We suggest that the wild component of Clade 3 is now extinct, while the extant guanacos derive from group which Clade 1 llamas originated from.
evidence: The manuscript proposes extinction of an ancestral lineage based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The extant guanacos derive from group which Clade 1 llamas originated from.
source: We suggest that the wild component of Clade 3 is now extinct, while the extant guanacos derive from group which Clade 1 llamas originated from.
evidence: The manuscript proposes evolutionary relationships based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The domestication scenario is consistent with the zooarchaeological and genetic evidence for multiple llama domestication centers across the Andes.
source: Such a scenario is consistent with the zooarchaeological and genetic evidence for multiple llama domestication centers across the Andes (Wheeler et al., 2006; Kadwell et al., 2001; Bruford et al., 2003), including sites in Northwestern Argentina and Northern Chile (Yacobaccio, 2001; Mengoni Goñalons and Yacobaccio, 2006; Cartajena, 2009; Núñez and Calogero, 1988; Olivera, 2001; Barreta et al., 2013) and in the Peruvian central Andes (Mengoni Goñalons and Yacobaccio, 2006; Moore, 2011).
evidence: The manuscript supports the proposed domestication scenario with citations to previous zooarchaeological and genetic studies.

claim: Alpacas may be the outcome of hybridization between llamas and vicuñas.
source: While that could have happened, it is also possible that alpacas are the outcome of hybridization between llamas and vicuñas (Wheeler, 1995; Wheeler, 2006; Renneberg, 2008).
evidence: The manuscript proposes a hybridization hypothesis for alpaca origin with citations to previous studies.

claim: Alpacas are assumed to have been domesticated independently of llama and probably earlier too.
source: Alpacas are assumed to have been domesticated independently of llama and probably earlier too (Wheeler, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research on alpaca domestication timing.

claim: Peruvian archaeological time series show the transition from human hunting of wild vicuñas and guanacos (9,000–6,000 years ago) to the establishment of early domestic forms (6,000–5,500 years ago).
source: Peruvian archaeological time series showing the transition from human hunting of wild vicuñas and guanacos (9,000–6,000 years ago) to the establishment of early domestic forms (6,000–5,500 years ago) and the development of human societies centered around pastoralism focused on alpacas and llamas management at high altitude starting 5,500 years ago (Wheeler, 1985; Wheeler, 1999).
evidence: The manuscript cites archaeological evidence for domestication timing from previous studies.

claim: The development of human societies centered around pastoralism focused on alpacas and llamas management at high altitude started 5,500 years ago.
source: Peruvian archaeological time series showing the transition from human hunting of wild vicuñas and guanacos (9,000–6,000 years ago) to the establishment of early domestic forms (6,000–5,500 years ago) and the development of human societies centered around pastoralism focused on alpacas and llamas management at high altitude starting 5,500 years ago (Wheeler, 1985; Wheeler, 1999).
evidence: The manuscript cites archaeological evidence for pastoralism development from previous studies.

claim: Pre-Columbian alpaca populations were substantially larger than today.
source: However, the archaeological evidence indicates that pre-Columbian alpaca populations were substantially larger than today and that a dramatic bottleneck occurred during the Spanish conquest (Wheeler, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites archaeological evidence for historical alpaca population sizes.

claim: A dramatic bottleneck occurred in alpaca populations during the Spanish conquest.
source: However, the archaeological evidence indicates that pre-Columbian alpaca populations were substantially larger than today and that a dramatic bottleneck occurred during the Spanish conquest (Wheeler, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites evidence for a population bottleneck during the Spanish conquest.

claim: Modern alpacas and llamas are the outcome of an extensive hybridization that has been attributed to the species near demise following the Spanish conquest.
source: Modern alpacas and llamas are the outcome of an extensive hybridization that has been attributed to the species near demise following the Spanish conquest (Kadwell et al., 2001; Casey et al., 2018; Fan et al., 2020), hybridization that so far has not been shown to have affected the wild SACs (i.e. guanaco and vicuña).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous genetic studies documenting post-conquest hybridization.

claim: Hybridization has not been shown to have affected the wild SACs (guanaco and vicuña).
source: Modern alpacas and llamas are the outcome of an extensive hybridization that has been attributed to the species near demise following the Spanish conquest (Kadwell et al., 2001; Casey et al., 2018; Fan et al., 2020), hybridization that so far has not been shown to have affected the wild SACs (i.e. guanaco and vicuña).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous genetic studies on hybridization patterns.

claim: During the Spanish conquest, camelid populations were drastically reduced.
source: During the Spanish conquest, camelid populations were drastically reduced (Gade, 2013), probably due to (i) a lack of understanding of the superior quality of their fiber for the textile industry, (ii) the interest in the introduction and establishment of cattle and sheep for the production of wool that was in high demand in the Low Countries, and (iii) as a measure to control local human populations by destabilizing their means of sustenance.
evidence: The manuscript cites historical evidence for camelid population decline during the Spanish conquest.

claim: Up to 40% of llamas show evidence of hybridization.
source: Hybridization between llamas and alpacas has become such an extensive issue that up to 40% of llamas and 80% of alpacas show evidence of hybridization (Kadwell et al., 2001), and through recent whole genome sequencing efforts, Fan et al., 2020 reported that up to 36% of the modern alpaca genome is likely derived from llama hybridization.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous genetic studies quantifying hybridization levels.

claim: Up to 80% of alpacas show evidence of hybridization.
source: Hybridization between llamas and alpacas has become such an extensive issue that up to 40% of llamas and 80% of alpacas show evidence of hybridization (Kadwell et al., 2001), and through recent whole genome sequencing efforts, Fan et al., 2020 reported that up to 36% of the modern alpaca genome is likely derived from llama hybridization.
